source.title: Scaling Laws for Discriminative Classification in Large Language Models
source.authors: Dean Wyatte; F. Tahmasbi; Ming Li; Thomas Markovich

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. It has some layout artifacts and placeholder ACM citation/DOI text, but is not cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether language-modeling performance predicts downstream classification performance, using a different task and measure from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: The paper reports domain-adaptation validation-loss curves in Figure 9 and classification-loss/accuracy scaling results in Figures 3 and 8 and Table 3. Its claims about classification loss are not held-out autoregressive pretraining loss; the direct link between domain-adaptation language-modeling loss and classification loss, and classification accuracy across model sizes, bears on V6. It does not fit a formal power law or test compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.test_reason: The paper reports its own results on whether downstream classification after closed-domain adaptation improves with Pythia size and domain-adaptation tokens. It also relates domain-adaptation LM loss to classification loss, which bears on V6. This is a new setting (discriminative classification of customer-support templates) rather than a replication of the original method, so T3 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that classification loss scales smoothly (linearly) with domain-adaptation tokens and is predictable from LM loss, and that larger models do better but cost latency, so smaller domain-adapted models trained longer are attractive. They explicitly say they do not fit a formal scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses closed-domain autoregressive adaptation of three Pythia sizes followed by supervised discriminative classification. It reports classification scaling relationships and validation-loss curves, but does not fit the original power-law forms, extrapolate larger runs, or search for a compute-optimal parameter/token split.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies model size, domain-adaptation token count and FLOPs, and domain-adaptation language-modeling loss. It also compares results with and without domain adaptation.
record.problems: The scaling experiments cover only three Pythia sizes and the customer-support domain. The paper does not fit scaling exponents or give uncertainty for the scaling curves, and several scaling results are presented in figures without numeric values. The authors say larger models were interrupted late in domain-adaptation training because of computational and time constraints.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional Top-3 and Top-5 accuracy values for the same Table 3 model/training conditions; these were omitted because Top-1 is the main accuracy measure retained for V6. Figures 8 and 9 are recorded as figure-only where relevant; no numerical values were inferred.

untested.parts: No from-scratch pretraining loss and no power-law fit over orders of magnitude.
No extrapolation from small to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation search. The authors only say the result is 'consistent with' compute-optimal work.
Domain-adaptation loss curves exist (Fig. 9) but no power-law form is fitted or tested.
Only three Pythia sizes (410m–2.8b), one domain and one task. No fitted law and no prediction of held-out larger models.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

missing.what: Stated equivalence: Pythia-1.4b at ~27B tokens matches the classification loss of Pythia-2.8b at ~3B tokens. This is a size/data trade-off on the downstream measure.
Authors' statement that domain adaptation (~4-5% accuracy) gives a larger uplift than the model-size increase at these scales.

record.verdict_notes: The evidence covers only a narrow range (~7x in parameters, under one order of magnitude in tokens). The relations are described as linear, not power-law, and the study is not an original source. R1–R3 are re-linked from V1 to V5 because they measure continued-pretraining loss.

versions.untested_parts: The paper plots domain-adaptation validation loss over training steps for three model sizes, but does not fit or report a power law, test compute scaling, or establish behavior over several orders of magnitude.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs is tested.
No fixed-compute search for an optimal parameter/token allocation is reported.
The study does not compare depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns text-domain adaptation and classification; it does not test other modalities or the listed repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer power-law forms.
The evidence is for customer-support template classification on three Pythia sizes; it does not establish downstream predictability across other tasks, model families, or much larger scales.
The study does not compare fitting choices or exponents, nor report curves bending away from a fitted power law.

relationships.condition: Domain-adapted Pythia 410m–2.8b, customer-support template classification, loss-based measures
relationships.reason: Classification loss falls with model size at matched FLOPs and tokens (R4, R5). The authors state a linear LM-loss-to-classification-loss relation across sizes (R6).
relationships.display_finding: Classification loss falls with model size at matched FLOPs and tokens and has a reported linear relationship with language-model loss.

relationships.condition: Pythia 410m–2.8b Top-1 accuracy, with and without domain adaptation
relationships.reason: Top-1 rises monotonically with size in both settings: 45.43→48.64→49.96% without adaptation (R12, R14, R16) and 51.09→53.75→55.12% with it (R13, R15, R17).
relationships.display_finding: Top-1 accuracy rises monotonically from 45.43% through 48.64% to 49.96% without adaptation and from 51.09% through 53.75% to 55.12% with adaptation.
